Two water levels, one gradient

Mekong above lake → inflow to the lake. Lake above Mekong → outflow. The lake stores water, so its peak follows the Mekong’s rise. The chart shows this lag and both crossings.

Module 1 · catchment water cycle

Turc (1954) estimates annual land evapotranspiration. The remaining rainfall splits into river runoff and groundwater recharge; this is a closed annual catchment budget.

The rest recharges groundwater. A teaching partition, not a soil infiltration model.

Effective river connection · Module 2.2

Q = sign(ΔH) × Cd × W × D × √(2g|ΔH|). ΔH = Mekong stage − lake stage. Equal stages give zero discharge; reversing the head reverses the flow.

This submerged-orifice equation is a lumped teaching approximation for the connection, not a Saint-Venant river model. Width and depth are effective parameters, not a river survey. Near-zero head is an idealized continuous limit, outside the cited measurement structure’s accuracy range.

Brief’s empirical reverse-volume rule

V = 41.5 × rainfall multiplier × (1 − 0.5 × dam regulation) × (1 − 0.4 × sand mining) km³/year.

This prescribed scenario rule is reported as a separate comparison. It is not a physical law, and is not imposed as an extra water source or sink on the head-driven/continuity calculation. The integrated hydraulic volume and this empirical estimate can differ.

Fisheries & livelihoods

Schaefer surplus production replaces the former fixed catch multiplier. Run years to see stock depletion or recovery.

Fish year 0

Fish biomass—tonnes · modeled
Last simulated annual catch—tonnes / completed year
Carrying capacity K—tonnes · annual habitat
Constant-K MSY reference—tonnes/year · rK/4

Biomass history (tonnes); each point is one completed fish year.

Flood pulse × remaining forest

Equations, inputs and limits

dB/dt = rB(1 − B/K) − H; H = qEB. B and K are tonnes, r is per year, q = 0.25 per year per unit effort, E is a dimensionless index. Monthly RK4 integration uses at least eight substeps per month (smaller adaptive steps when biomass greatly exceeds capacity) and accounts for biological growth, harvest, and stock change.

K = K₀ × annual flooded-forest area-days / natural area-days × remaining forest fraction. K₀ = 4.8 million tonnes; initial B = 2.4 million tonnes. Annual habitat averaging avoids a zero carrying capacity in the dry season. It does not resolve species, migration, or monthly nursery effects. If no forest habitat remains, zero capacity is treated as complete stock loss in the next step, recorded as biological loss rather than harvest; this is an explicit teaching boundary assumption. Clearing reduces capacity proportionally to remaining mapped forest; spatial differences within that forest are not resolved.

At reference r = 0.5, K = 4.8 million and E = 1, B = K/2 and catch = MSY = 600,000 t/year. This is a classroom calibration to the requested range, not an observed stock estimate. All fish parameters are illustrative. For effort fishing, persistent qE > r drives collapse; a fixed quota above rK/4 also causes collapse but is a different harvest policy.

Fish runs hold current climate and land cover fixed. Land-year steps also advance fish one year after updating habitat. Changing sliders changes future runs; reset fish to compare from the same initial stock. The seasonal Play button remains a hydrology animation.

FAO: Schaefer surplus production

Bon Om Touk · Water Festival

Boat races and riverfront celebrations mark the seasonal transition toward the lake’s return flow. The festival usually falls in October or November on the lunar calendar; it does not set the hydrological reversal date.

A nursery among the trees

Flooded forest provides shelter, food and rearing habitat. Many fish use the floodplain to feed and grow; breeding and migration differ among species. A longer, connected flood pulse can support more productive habitat.

Dams, sand and livelihoods

Flow regulation can flatten seasonal peaks and interrupt migration or sediment supply. Riverbed incision associated with sand mining can lower Mekong water levels and weaken reverse flow. Forest loss, fishing pressure and weather also matter; this model isolates only a few mechanisms.

Population-equivalent assumptions

Catch × 1,000 kg/t × 60% assumed locally available share ÷ 57.8 kg/person/year fish consumption. This is an annual food-supply equivalent, not a count of actual residents, jobs, or people fully supported. The consumption reference comes from an IFReDI study reported by MRC; the 60% share is a classroom assumption.

Sources: Conservation International · WCS · Water Festival

Land use · annual change

A Markov chain sets conversion amounts. A cellular automaton places growth using neighbors, distance to town, and modeled flooding.

Year 0

ClassInitial km²Now km²

More paving, less recharge

The Water balance runoff slider is the year-zero reference. The applied fraction increases with added urban area. This model changes annual runoff volume; storm peaks and travel times are not simulated.

Annual transition matrix

Rows = from; columns = to. W water, F forest, A farmland, U urban. All row sums equal 1.

Default illustrative rates: forest → farmland 2.5%, forest → urban 0.6%, farmland → urban 1.8% per year. Water and existing urban land persist. Protection reduces forest conversion only. Largest-remainder rounding allocates whole cells; fractional Markov targets can differ by fewer than two cells per class per step.

Methods and assumptions

Urban suitability = 0.45 × neighboring urban fraction + 0.30 / (1 + distance to existing urban cells) + 0.25 × (1 − flood frequency). Distances use grid cells; neighborhoods use eight adjacent cells. Scores are evaluated synchronously each year. Highest-scoring eligible cells convert first.

This is an illustrative classification traced from the reference, not remotely sensed land cover. Permanent-water land class is fixed; seasonal inundation does not permanently convert ownership or land cover. Cell flood thresholds are synthetic. Each land year recomputes an equilibrated seasonal hydrology cycle; this is not continuous multi-year reservoir routing. The hydrology flooded-forest metric represents potential seasonal inundation; Module 2.4 discounts this by remaining forest fraction for fish habitat. Runoff feedback uses the 70,000 km² terrestrial catchment; permanent water is additional mapped area.

Population & dry-season water

Illustrative regional population starts at 3 million. Logistic growth approaches a planning ceiling; demand combines households, irrigated farmland, and an industry proxy.

Town year 0

Regional population—people · illustrative
Dry-season demand—km³ / 120 days
Demand sectorkm³ / 120 days

Available storage proxy—km³ after reserve
Demand / storage—dimensionless

Population history, one point per town year. Town-only runs hold land use and climate fixed. Land-year steps also advance population. Sliders apply prospectively; reset population for a fresh comparison.

Equations and assumptions

Logistic growth: P(t)=K/[1+((K−P₀)/P₀)e^(−rt)]. Each year uses current population as P₀, so changing r or K does not rewrite history. An initial population above K declines toward K.

Demand = P × household use + irrigated hectares × crop demand + P × industry factor, integrated over 120 days. 1 km² = 100 ha; 1 L = 0.001 m³. Crop input is gross irrigation demand, with delivery losses folded into that illustrative input.

Supply proxy = minimum modeled lake storage during days 0–119 (January–April) × (1 − reserve fraction). This is a stock-based stress scenario, not renewable annual supply, an abstraction permit, or a routed water-allocation model. Demand is not withdrawn from the hydrological solver, and return flows are not modeled. The reserve is a teaching fraction of storage, not a measured environmental-flow requirement.

Demand / storage > 0.4 triggers the brief’s classroom high-pressure marker; above 1 demand exceeds the available stock proxy. At zero supply the ratio is undefined and shown as “No supply.” These labels are not official FAO SDG categories. All population, irrigation and industry parameters are mock inputs.

Town flood depth & damage

A representative site at the Phnom Penh confluence uses the modeled Mekong stage. Move the seasonal timeline or play the year to see water cross the floor level.

Water above floor—m · selected date
Damage fraction—of exposed value
Selected-stage damage—million USD · scenario
Annual peak-stage damage—million USD · one event

Damage curve · depth above floor (m). Dot marks the selected date. Peak and current damage are alternative event estimates; they are not added across dates.

Method and assumptions

Depth = max(0, Mekong stage − ground elevation − floor raise). All levels share the hydrology model datum, not a surveyed elevation datum. A single representative confluence site is used; no street-level flood routing or levees are modeled.

Fraction = 0 for depth ≤ 0; 0.4 × depth from 0 to 2 m; 0.8 + 0.1 × (depth − 2) from 2 to 4 m; capped at 1 above 4 m. Damage = fraction × exposed asset value. The curve is monotonic and bounded.

The depth-damage method follows standard practice, but this curve, ground level, floor raise and asset value are illustrative. This is conditional event damage, not probability-weighted expected annual loss. Flood duration, velocity, vulnerability differences, indirect losses and repeated-event recovery are omitted. Asset value stays fixed unless adjusted; it is not inferred from regional population or urban area.

JRC: Global flood depth-damage functions (2017)

Model, calibration and source notes

Module 1 water cycle: Turc (1954) annual actual evapotranspiration and catchment/reservoir water-balance equations. Turc uses ET = min(P, P/√(0.9 + (P/L)²)), L = 300 + 25T + 0.05T³, with P and ET in mm/year and T in °C. Annual land storage change is assumed zero: P = ET + runoff + recharge. Recharge is retained outside the lake model; it is not counted twice as river inflow.

Lake integration: a repeating 365-day balance, six-hour backward-Euler steps, seven spin-up years. ΔV = (river exchange + catchment runoff − net lake atmospheric loss) × Δt. Effective orifice connection width is fitted so positive annual exchange integrates to 41.5 km³ in the reference. One pressure bundle is fitted to 29.3 km³. Neither fit validates timing, geometry, causal attribution or the flood map. Module 2.2 uses submerged-orifice discharge with the lake stage solved from storage; Manning remains available in the Module 1 source library.

Observed versus illustrative: only the two period-average reverse-flow targets are observational constraints here. Mock values: reference rainfall 1,600 mm/year, mean temperature 27 °C, terrestrial catchment 70,000 km², runoff share 75%, effective discharge coefficient Cd = 0.70, effective depth 3 m and g = 9.81 m/s². Channel width is fitted, not surveyed. Net lake atmospheric loss is held at 110 m³/s and is separate from land Turc ET.

Inherited assumptions: synthetic area–stage curve A(H) = 1,800 + 1,300H km²; its storage integral V(H) = (1.8H + 0.65H²) × 10⁹ m³. Synthetic monthly forcing uses smooth interpolation. The runoff shape is normalized to the Turc catchment's annual runoff volume. Dam smoothing, stage incision and downstream backwater offsets remain teaching parameterizations. The empirical reverse-volume multiplier from the brief is a separate comparison, not an additional conservation equation.

Forest and fisheries: an assumed 3,300 km² forest ring floods progressively between lake stages 3.0 and 8.3 m. Annual catch scales as (scenario forest area-days / baseline forest area-days)0.65, capped at 1.6× the baseline. The exponent, habitat capacity and availability share are assumptions. Both catch ranges are scaling ranges, not confidence intervals. No fishing-effort, migration-barrier, temperature or species model is included.

Visuals: the original reference image is projected onto inferred relief. A separate blue water mesh rises over a traced basin. Flood extent is illustrative and does not establish a surveyed stage–area map. Levels use a shared model bed datum, not field gauge readings. The water color is chosen for clarity. Villages are illustrative markers; camera rotation is limited because unseen geometry is inferred.

  • Sand-mining-driven reduction in Tonle Sap Lake’s critical flood pulse, Nature Sustainability (2025): 41.5 versus 29.3 km³ reverse-flow benchmarks.
  • Mekong River Commission: seasonal flow-reversal mechanism.
  • Conservation International Cambodia: lake fisheries estimate of 300,000–500,000 tonnes/year. WCS reports a lower range, illustrating source and scope differences.
  • MRC fisheries report: 57.8 kg/person/year consumption from IFReDI (2013); national production figures should not be confused with lake-only catch.

Equation references: IIASA: annual Turc relation · USACE: Manning equation. Module 2.6 adds illustrative conditional flood damage at one representative town site.
